summary: orca: orchestration for Mojo data pipelines.
description:
Declare steps and the pipeline they make, and give the binary orca's
command line:

```mojo
from dista import Seq
from orca import Ctx, Gather, Mapped, Month, Pipeline, Step, orca_main

def size(mut ctx: Ctx, m: Month) raises -> Int:
    return m.month * 100

def total(mut ctx: Ctx, sizes: Seq[Int]) raises -> Int:
    var t = 0
    for i in range(len(sizes)):
        t += sizes[i]
    return t

comptime Size = Step["size", Month, Int, size, Mapped]
comptime Total = Step["total", Seq[Int], Int, total, Gather, after=Size]
comptime Sizes = Pipeline["sizes", Size, Total]

def main() raises:
    orca_main[Sizes]()
```

See DESIGN.md for how it works and where it's going.

modules.summary: What `orca ui` does to runs: each action is rows in Postgres that the scheduler, or the run's own process, acts on.
modules.description:
The UI never starts a pipeline's binary. Starting, resuming, rerunning and
backfilling leave a `queued` run, which the scheduler starts on its next
tick as it starts any other, within `max_runs`; cancelling sets
`cancel_requested`, which a running run sees before its next attempt (an
attempt already going finishes). So the UI works the same wherever the
scheduler runs, and retries and limits stay in one place.

Each action returns an `Outcome`: the run it made or acted on, or why it
refused, which is something the person can fix (a bad range, a run that's
still going) rather than an error.

fields.name: run
fields.summary: The run made or acted on; 0 when refused, or for a backfill.

fields.name: queued
fields.summary: How many runs a backfill queued.

fields.name: refused
fields.summary: Why the action wasn't done, or empty.

fields.name: confirm
fields.summary: Refused only until confirmed: a resume onto new code.

overloads.signature: def done(run: Int, queued: Int = Int(0)) -> Self
def no(var why: String, confirm: Bool = False) -> Self

overloads.summary: `ORCA_STALE_SECONDS` (default 30): how old a running run's heartbeat is when its process is taken to have died.
True for a run that's `running` with no live process: its heartbeat, or its start when it has none yet, is older than the stale limit.

overloads.signature: def start_run(mut db: State, pipeline: String, keys: String) -> Outcome
overloads.summary: A queued run over the partitions in `keys`, trigger `ui`.

overloads.signature: def backfill_runs(mut db: State, pipeline: String, keys: String, rerun: Bool = False) -> Outcome
overloads.summary: What `orca backfill` does: queued runs, `keys_per_run` keys each, of the keys in `keys` that aren't done and aren't in a live run; for time keys, by default a run for each partition in `keys` that has none queued, running or succeeded. With `rerun`, done keys are queued too.

overloads.signature: def resume_run(mut db: State, run: Int, allow_new_code: Bool) -> Outcome
overloads.summary: Queues a failed, cancelled or stalled run again, so the scheduler resumes it at what's unfinished. A run whose pipeline's code has changed since is refused until `allow_new_code`, which the scheduler passes on as `--allow-new-code`.

overloads.signature: def rerun_from(mut db: State, run: Int, step: String) -> Outcome
overloads.summary: A new queued run over the same partitions, trigger `rerun`, with the steps before `step` that succeeded copied from `run` (their outputs, and `copied_from` naming the step they came from, whose attempts, reads and commits stay with it). Resuming it runs `step` and what follows. `run` is left as it was.

overloads.signature: def cancel_run(mut db: State, run: Int) -> Outcome
overloads.summary: Cancels a run: a queued or failed one at once (a failed one isn't retried), a running one before its next attempt.

overloads.signature: def rebuild_downstream(mut db: State, dataset: String, keys: String) -> Outcome
overloads.summary: What `orca rebuild` does: plans runs of every pipeline downstream of `dataset` over `keys`, which the scheduler queues a level at a time. The outcome's `run` is the rebuild's ID.

modules.summary: Who may act in `orca ui`: users with passwords, their sessions, and a record of what each did.
modules.description:
```
orca user add alice       reads the password from standard input
orca user remove alice    and ends their sessions
orca user list
```

Anyone who can reach the UI can read it. Its actions (start, backfill,
resume, rerun, cancel, rebuild) need a logged-in user once login is on:
when `ORCA_UI_LOGIN=required`, or as soon as any user exists, so a
deployment can't be left open by forgetting the variable once it has users.

Passwords are kept as bcrypt hashes made by Postgres's pgcrypto
(`crypt(password, gen_salt('bf', 12))`), so neither orca nor its logs see
one after it's checked. Logging in makes a session: 32 random bytes from
the system's generator, given to the browser as the cookie `orca_session`
and kept only as their SHA-256 digest, for `ORCA_UI_SESSION_HOURS` (default
12). Every action a user takes is a row of `orca.audit`, and so is every failed
login, which `too_many_failures` counts: after 5 for one name, or 20 from
one address, in 15 minutes, `/login` answers 429 without checking a
password, so a public UI can't be guessed at.

overloads.signature: def add_user(mut db: State, name: String, password: String) -> Bool
overloads.summary: Adds the user, or sets an existing one's password (ending her sessions); True if the user is new.

overloads.signature: def remove_user(mut db: State, name: String) -> Bool
overloads.summary: Removes the user and their sessions; False if there was none.

overloads.signature: def too_many_failures(mut db: State, name: String, address: String) -> Bool
overloads.summary: Whether logins for `name`, or from `address`, have failed too often of late to check another: `FAILURES_PER_NAME` for a name or `FAILURES_PER_ADDRESS` from an address in `FAILURE_WINDOW_MINUTES`. Failures are `login-failed` rows of `orca.audit`, with the address as their detail.

overloads.signature: def login_failed(mut db: State, name: String, address: String)
def open_session(mut db: State, name: String, password: String) -> String
overloads.summary: A new session's token if the password is the user's, else empty.

overloads.signature: def session_user(mut db: State, token: String) -> String
overloads.summary: The user whose session `token` is, or empty.

overloads.signature: def close_session(mut db: State, token: String)
def audit(mut db: State, user: String, action: String, run: Int, detail: String)
overloads.summary: Records that `user` did `action` (the action's path), to `run` (0 for none), with `detail` (what the form gave).

modules.summary: `orca aws`: a project's orca on AWS, with the `aws` and `docker` commands its user already has (`aws login`, or `AWS_PROFILE` for a named profile).
modules.description:
orca aws up --email you@example.com [--stack orca] [--hostname H]
                [--console-hostname H] [--budget 100] [--zone us-east-2a]
    orca aws push [--tag T]                     # the project's image, to ECR
    orca aws register [--tag T] [register flags] <pipeline> [...]
    orca aws app <name> [--host H] [--port 8080] [--tag T]
    orca aws status
    orca aws down --yes

`up` creates or updates the stack from the template orca carries
(deploy/aws/orca.yaml, in `orca.aws_assets`); the first time it needs
`--email`, for the Budgets alert, and makes the database's password. `push`
builds the project's image from a staged copy of `pixi.toml`, `pixi.lock`,
`bin/`, `pipelines/` and `src/`, with the project's `Dockerfile.orca` or
else the template (deploy/project.Dockerfile), for arm64, tagged with the
commit (or `--tag`) and `latest`, and pushes it to the stack's repository.
`register` and `app` run on the control instance through SSM: `register`
moves the scheduler and the UI to the image (`orca-refresh`) and registers
each pipeline, `/opt/orca/pipelines/<pipeline>`, with the flags given, as
`orca register` takes them; `app` runs the image's `/opt/orca/bin/<name>`
beside the UI, at `https://<host>` (for `console`, the stack's
`ConsoleHostname`). `down` deletes the stack, which fails while its buckets
hold objects.

Files go to `build/orca-aws/`. `--stack` (default `orca`) and `--region`
(default `AWS_REGION`, else the `aws` command's own) go anywhere.

aliases.name: AWS_USAGE
aliases.value:
"usage:
  orca aws up --email ADDR [--hostname H] [--console-hostname H] [--budget N]
              [--zone AZ]
  orca aws push [--tag T]
  orca aws register [--tag T] [register flags] <pipeline> [...]
  orca aws app <name> [--host H] [--port 8080] [--tag T]
  orca aws status
  orca aws down --yes
  (each takes --stack NAME, default orca, and --region R)"

overloads.summary: `orca aws <cmd> ...`: `args` is the whole command line.

modules.summary: The stack template and the project Dockerfile `orca aws` writes out: deploy/aws/orca.yaml and deploy/project.Dockerfile, embedded by scripts/embed-aws.py. Edit those, then run it; `pixi run test-aws-assets` fails while this is out of date.

aliases.name: STACK_TEMPLATE
aliases.value:
StringSpan("# orca on AWS with the ec2 runner (DESIGN.md, phase 5, PR 5b): one stack,
# so it's reviewed as one file and deleted as one stack.
#
# - a VPC with one public subnet in the Availability Zone given, and a
#   gateway endpoint for S3;
# - the control instance: the scheduler (ORCA_RUNNER=ec2), Postgres and
#   orca ui as containers, Caddy in front with a Let's Encrypt certificate;
# - what runs need: a bucket for the warehouse and logs, a repository for
#   the image, a role and profile for run instances, a security group they
#   share;
# - a public bucket, mlake-public-<account>, for data anyone may read
#   unsigned (the project's resource control policy refuses other accounts'
#   signed requests): the warehouse, ORCA_WAREHOUSE, is in it, since a
#   demo's tables are meant to be read; orca's own bucket keeps the logs;
# - the console's hostname, served by the same Caddy from a container
#   named console on port 8080, once one runs;
# - a Budgets alert.
#
# orca ui is public for reading, as a demo is; its actions need a login
# (orca user add, in the scheduler's container). Nothing else accepts a
# connection from outside: Postgres takes the run instances' only, and the
# instances take each other's only.
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: \222010-09-09\22
Description: orca with the ec2 runner, a control instance and runs on instances of their own

Parameters:
  AvailabilityZone:
    Type: AWS::EC2::AvailabilityZone::Name
    Default: us-east-2a
  ControlInstanceType:
    Type: String
    Default: t4g.large
  AllowedRunTypes:
    Type: CommaDelimitedList
    Default: \22c7g.large,c7g.xlarge,c7g.2xlarge,c7g.4xlarge,t4g.medium,t4g.large\22
    Description: The only instance types the scheduler may start
  Ami:
    Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id>
    Default: /aws/service/ecs/optimized-ami/amazon-linux-2023/arm64/recommended/image_id
    Description: arm64 Amazon Linux 2023 with Docker, for the control and run instances
  ImageTag:
    Type: String
    Default: latest
    Description: The tag of the orca image the control instance starts with (orca aws push pushes latest)
  ConsoleHostname:
    Type: String
    Default: libs.mlake.dev
    Description: The console app's hostname, an A record to PublicAddress; empty for none
  Hostname:
    Type: String
    Default: orca-demo.mlake.dev
    Description: The UI's public name, an A record to PublicAddress; it answers at <PublicAddress>.sslip.io too
  DbPassword:
    Type: String
    NoEcho: true
    MinLength: 16
    # It goes into a shell script and a URL as it is.
    AllowedPattern: \22[A-Za-z0-9]+\22
  BudgetEmail:
    Type: String
  BudgetDollars:
    Type: Number
    Default: 100

Resources:
  Vpc:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPC
    Properties:
      CidrBlock: 10.42.0.0/16
      EnableDnsHostnames: true
      EnableDnsSupport: true
      Tags: [{Key: Name, Value: orca}]
  Subnet:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Subnet
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      CidrBlock: 10.42.0.0/20
      AvailabilityZone: !Ref AvailabilityZone
      MapPublicIpOnLaunch: true
      Tags: [{Key: Name, Value: orca}]
  Gateway:
    Type: AWS::EC2::InternetGateway
  GatewayAttachment:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPCGatewayAttachment
    Properties: {VpcId: !Ref Vpc, InternetGatewayId: !Ref Gateway}
  Routes:
    Type: AWS::EC2::RouteTable
    Properties: {VpcId: !Ref Vpc}
  DefaultRoute:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Route
    DependsOn: GatewayAttachment
    Properties: {RouteTableId: !Ref Routes, DestinationCidrBlock: 0.0.0.0/0, GatewayId: !Ref Gateway}
  SubnetRoutes:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SubnetRouteTableAssociation
    Properties: {SubnetId: !Ref Subnet, RouteTableId: !Ref Routes}
  # S3 traffic stays in the region, and costs nothing.
  S3Endpoint:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPCEndpoint
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      ServiceName: !Sub com.amazonaws.${AWS::Region}.s3
      VpcEndpointType: Gateway
      RouteTableIds: [!Ref Routes]

  Bucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub orca-${AWS::AccountId}-${AWS::Region}
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault: {SSEAlgorithm: AES256}
      LifecycleConfiguration:
        Rules:
          - {Id: logs, Status: Enabled, Prefix: logs/, ExpirationInDays: 30}
  # Data anyone may read: the lake's public tables. Account-level Block
  # Public Access, if it's on, refuses the policy below.
  PublicBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub mlake-public-${AWS::AccountId}
      OwnershipControls:
        Rules: [{ObjectOwnership: BucketOwnerEnforced}]
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: false
        RestrictPublicBuckets: false
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault: {SSEAlgorithm: AES256}
      # Browsers, such as DuckDB in a page, read it too.
      CorsConfiguration:
        CorsRules:
          - {AllowedMethods: [GET, HEAD], AllowedOrigins: [\22*\22], AllowedHeaders: [\22*\22], MaxAge: 3600}
  PublicBucketPolicy:
    Type: AWS::S3::BucketPolicy
    Properties:
      Bucket: !Ref PublicBucket
      PolicyDocument:
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: \22*\22
            Action: s3:GetObject
            Resource: !Sub ${PublicBucket.Arn}/*
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: \22*\22
            Action: s3:ListBucket
            Resource: !GetAtt PublicBucket.Arn

  Repository:
    Type: AWS::ECR::Repository
    Properties:
      RepositoryName: orca
      ImageScanningConfiguration: {ScanOnPush: true}
      LifecyclePolicy:
        LifecyclePolicyText: |
          {\22rules\22: [{\22rulePriority\22: 1, \22description\22: \22keep the last 5\22,
            \22selection\22: {\22tagStatus\22: \22any\22, \22countType\22: \22imageCountMoreThan\22, \22countNumber\22: 5},
            \22action\22: {\22type\22: \22expire\22}}]}

  RunGroup:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
    Properties:
      GroupDescription: orca run instances, which talk to each other only
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
  RunGroupSelf:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroupIngress
    Properties:
      GroupId: !Ref RunGroup
      SourceSecurityGroupId: !Ref RunGroup
      IpProtocol: tcp
      FromPort: 0
      ToPort: 65535
  # The scheduler reads a scaling run's demand from its head (dista's port).
  RunGroupHead:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroupIngress
    Properties:
      GroupId: !Ref RunGroup
      SourceSecurityGroupId: !Ref ControlGroup
      IpProtocol: tcp
      FromPort: 6390
      ToPort: 6390
  ControlGroup:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
    Properties:
      GroupDescription: orca control instance, public for HTTPS only
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      SecurityGroupIngress:
        - {IpProtocol: tcp, FromPort: 80, ToPort: 80, CidrIp: 0.0.0.0/0}
        - {IpProtocol: tcp, FromPort: 443, ToPort: 443, CidrIp: 0.0.0.0/0}
        - {IpProtocol: tcp, FromPort: 5432, ToPort: 5432, SourceSecurityGroupId: !Ref RunGroup}

  RunRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Statement: [{Effect: Allow, Principal: {Service: ec2.amazonaws.com}, Action: sts:AssumeRole}]
      ManagedPolicyArns: [arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore]
      Policies:
        # Runs' secrets (orca register --secret), only those under orca/.
        - PolicyName: secrets
          PolicyDocument:
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: secretsmanager:GetSecretValue
                Resource: !Sub arn:aws:secretsmanager:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:secret:orca/*
        - PolicyName: bucket-and-image
          PolicyDocument:
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: [s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, s3:DeleteObject]
                Resource: [!Sub \22${Bucket.Arn}/*\22, !Sub \22${PublicBucket.Arn}/*\22]
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: s3:ListBucket
                Resource: [!GetAtt Bucket.Arn, !GetAtt PublicBucket.Arn]
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: [ecr:BatchGetImage, ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer]
                Resource: !GetAtt Repository.Arn
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ecr:GetAuthorizationToken
                Resource: \22*\22
  RunProfile:
    Type: AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile
    Properties: {Roles: [!Ref RunRole]}

  ControlRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Statement: [{Effect: Allow, Principal: {Service: ec2.amazonaws.com}, Action: sts:AssumeRole}]
      ManagedPolicyArns: [arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore]
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: run-instances
          PolicyDocument:
            Statement:
              # Only instances tagged for orca, of the allowed types, from
              # the stack's AMI, in its subnet and group, with its profile.
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ec2:RunInstances
                Resource: !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:instance/*
                Condition:
                  StringEquals: {ec2:InstanceType: !Ref AllowedRunTypes}
                  \22Null\22: {\22aws:RequestTag/orca.run\22: \22false\22}
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ec2:RunInstances
                Resource:
                  - !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:volume/*
                  - !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:network-interface/*
                  - !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:subnet/${Subnet}
                  - !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:security-group/${RunGroup}
                  - !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}::image/*
                  - !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:spot-instances-request/*
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ec2:CreateTags
                Resource: !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:*/*
                Condition:
                  StringEquals: {ec2:CreateAction: RunInstances}
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ec2:TerminateInstances
                Resource: !Sub arn:aws:ec2:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:instance/*
                Condition:
                  \22Null\22: {\22aws:ResourceTag/orca.run\22: \22false\22}
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ec2:DescribeInstances
                Resource: \22*\22
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: iam:PassRole
                Resource: !GetAtt RunRole.Arn
        - PolicyName: bucket-and-image
          PolicyDocument:
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: [s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, s3:DeleteObject]
                Resource: [!Sub \22${Bucket.Arn}/*\22, !Sub \22${PublicBucket.Arn}/*\22]
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: s3:ListBucket
                Resource: [!GetAtt Bucket.Arn, !GetAtt PublicBucket.Arn]
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: [ecr:BatchGetImage, ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer]
                Resource: !GetAtt Repository.Arn
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: ecr:GetAuthorizationToken
                Resource: \22*\22
  ControlProfile:
    Type: AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile
    Properties: {Roles: [!Ref ControlRole]}

  ControlAddress:
    Type: AWS::EC2::EIP
    Properties: {Domain: vpc}
  Control:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
    DependsOn: DefaultRoute
    Properties:
      ImageId: !Ref Ami
      InstanceType: !Ref ControlInstanceType
      SubnetId: !Ref Subnet
      SecurityGroupIds: [!Ref ControlGroup]
      IamInstanceProfile: !Ref ControlProfile
      MetadataOptions: {HttpTokens: required, HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 2}
      BlockDeviceMappings:
        - DeviceName: /dev/xvda
          Ebs: {VolumeSize: 40, VolumeType: gp3, Encrypted: true}
      Tags: [{Key: Name, Value: orca-control}]
      UserData:
        Fn::Base64: !Sub
          - |
            #!/bin/bash
            # orca's control instance: Postgres, the scheduler, the UI and
            # Caddy, as containers that restart with the instance.
            set -eux
            # Docker without ECS: this AMI's agent would look for a cluster.
            systemctl disable --now ecs || true
            systemctl enable --now docker
            command -v aws || dnf install -y awscli
            token=$(curl -sX PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token -H 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 300')
            md() { curl -s -H \22X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $token\22 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/$1; }
            ip=$(md local-ipv4)
            # The Elastic IP's sslip.io name works at once; the hostname once
            # its A record points here. Caddy gets a certificate for each.
            sslip=\22$(echo ${PublicIp} | tr . -).sslip.io\22
            hosts=\22$sslip\22
            [ -z \22${Hostname}\22 ] || hosts=\22${Hostname}, $sslip\22
            registry=${AWS::AccountId}.dkr.ecr.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com
            image=$registry/orca:${ImageTag}
            login=\22command -v aws >/dev/null || dnf install -y awscli; systemctl disable --now ecs || true; aws ecr get-login-password --region ${AWS::Region} | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $registry\22
            # The image is pushed after the stack is made, so wait for it.
            until sh -c \22$login\22 && docker pull $image; do sleep 30; done
            docker network create orca || true
            mkdir -p /var/lib/orca/pg /var/lib/orca/caddy /var/lib/orca/stage
            docker run -d --name postgres --restart always --network orca -p 5432:5432 \
              -e POSTGRES_USER=orca -e POSTGRES_DB=orca -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD='${DbPassword}' \
              -v /var/lib/orca/pg:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17-bookworm -c synchronous_commit=on
            until docker exec postgres pg_isready -U orca -d orca; do sleep 2; done
            cat > /etc/orca.env << EOF
            ORCA_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://orca:${DbPassword}@postgres:5432/orca
            ORCA_EC2_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://orca:${DbPassword}@$ip:5432/orca
            ORCA_RUNNER=ec2
            AWS_REGION=${AWS::Region}
            ORCA_EC2_AMI=${Ami}
            ORCA_EC2_SUBNET=${Subnet}
            ORCA_EC2_SECURITY_GROUP=${RunGroup}
            ORCA_EC2_PROFILE=${RunProfile}
            ORCA_EC2_PREAMBLE=$login
            ORCA_WAREHOUSE=s3://${PublicBucket}/warehouse
            ORCA_LOGS=s3://${Bucket}/logs
            ORCA_PUBLIC_WAREHOUSE=s3://${PublicBucket}/warehouse
            ORCA_RUN_ENV=ORCA_PUBLIC_WAREHOUSE
            ORCA_LOG_STAGE=/var/lib/orca/stage
            ORCA_UI_ADDR=0.0.0.0:8270
            ORCA_UI_LOGIN=required
            ORCA_UI_SECURE_COOKIES=1
            ORCA_UI_TRUST_PROXY=1
            EOF
            # orca aws register and orca aws app run these over SSM.
            cat > /usr/local/bin/orca-refresh << 'EOS'
            #!/bin/bash
            # orca-refresh [TAG]: pull the orca image at TAG (else the last
            # one) and run the scheduler and the UI from it again.
            set -eu

aliases.value:
StringSpan("# The image `orca aws push` builds for a project that added orca with
# `pixi shelf add orca-mojo`: its own `orca` (bin/scheduler.mojo, the two
# lines calling orca.command), its apps (every other bin/*.mojo, at
# /opt/orca/bin/<name>, which `orca aws app` runs) and its pipelines (every
# pipelines/*.mojo, at /opt/orca/pipelines/<name>), with `src/` on the
# import path if the project has one. A project with a Dockerfile.orca of
# its own builds that instead.
#
# ORCA_SOURCE and ORCA_COMMIT say what the pipelines were built from, which
# each run records and orca ui links.
FROM ghcr.io/prefix-dev/pixi:0.78.0 AS build
ARG ORCA_SOURCE=\22\22
ARG ORCA_COMMIT=\22\22
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc libc6-dev git ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /src/project
COPY pixi.toml pixi.lock ./
RUN pixi install --locked
COPY . .
RUN mkdir -p /out/bin /out/pipelines \
    && pixi run sh -c 'inc=\22\22; [ -d src ] && inc=\22-I src\22; \
        [ -f bin/scheduler.mojo ] || { echo \22orca aws push: no bin/scheduler.mojo calling orca.command\22; exit 1; }; \
        for f in bin/*.mojo; do n=$(basename \22$f\22 .mojo); [ \22$n\22 = scheduler ] && n=orca; \
            mojo build $inc \22$f\22 -o \22/out/bin/$n\22 || exit 1; done; \
        for p in pipelines/*.mojo; do [ -f \22$p\22 ] || continue; n=$(basename \22$p\22 .mojo); \
            mojo build $inc -D ORCA_SOURCE='\22${ORCA_SOURCE}\22' -D ORCA_COMMIT='\22${ORCA_COMMIT}\22' \
                \22$p\22 -o \22/out/pipelines/$n\22 || exit 1; done; \
        if ls /out/pipelines/* > /dev/null 2>&1; then /out/bin/orca locate /out/pipelines/* --root .; fi'
# Only the pixi environment's libraries the binaries link or dlopen: libpq
# (postgres), flare's shims (orca ui, apps), and every tin's shim, such as
# objectstore's and the codecs' (zstd, for Iceberg writes).
RUN env=/src/project/.pixi/envs/default && mkdir -p /out/lib \
    && loaded=$(ls $env/lib/libpq.so* $env/lib/libflare_*.so $env/lib/lib*mojo*.so 2>/dev/null) \
    && ldd /out/bin/* /out/pipelines/* $loaded 2> /dev/null | awk -v e=\22$env\22 '$3 ~ \22^\22e {print $3}' \
        | sort -u | xargs -r cp -L -t /out/lib \
    && cp -L -t /out/lib $loaded

FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tzdata ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY --from=build /out/lib /opt/orca/lib
COPY --from=build /out/bin /opt/orca/bin
COPY --from=build /out/pipelines /opt/orca/pipelines
ENV CONDA_PREFIX=/opt/orca LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/orca/lib PATH=/opt/orca/bin:/opt/orca/pipelines:/usr/bin:/bin
ENTRYPOINT [\22/opt/orca/bin/orca\22]
")

modules.summary: `orca_main`: the command line every pipeline binary gets.
modules.description:
```
taxi describe                              the DAG as JSON
taxi run --partitions 2024-01..2024-03     starts a run and runs it
taxi resume <run> [--allow-new-code]       continues a run at what's unfinished
taxi status [<run>]                        the latest runs, or one run's steps
taxi sense                                 the current snapshot of each dataset it reads
labels keys                                a keyed pipeline's keys snapshot, then its keys
```

For a keyed pipeline (`orca.keyed`), `--partitions` takes names: a list,
`@all` or `@file:<path>`. A name its keys dataset doesn't have now is
refused, as a malformed key is, with exit code 2.

With `ORCA_DATABASE_URL` set, runs are recorded in Postgres and can be
resumed; without it, `run` runs in memory and `resume` and `status` aren't
available. `ORCA_STALE_SECONDS` (default 30) is how old a run's heartbeat must
be before another process may resume it.

A pipeline with dista tasks gets a runtime per run, started before anything
else so its forked processes inherit no connection or thread; run with
`DISTA_ROLE` set, the binary is a dista head or worker instead (see
`orca.tasks`). With `ORCA_LOGS` set, a directory or a location in object
storage (`orca.logs`), attempts log there, the run's dista timeline is
written beside them, and `status <run>` shows each step's latest log.

`sense` prints a line per dataset the pipeline reads and doesn't write,
`<dataset> <snapshot> <orca|other> <partitions|->`: its table's current
snapshot in `ORCA_WAREHOUSE` (-1 for none), whether an orca step made it,
and the partition keys its summary says it holds. The scheduler polls it for
a sensor pipeline (`orca.sensors`).

`run` and `resume` print one line per step and partition, then the run's
status. Exit codes: 0 when the run succeeded, 1 when a step didn't or the run
was cancelled, 2 for a
usage error, 3 for any other error (the database, a run that can't be
resumed).

modules.summary: Cron expressions, and when they next fire in a time zone.
modules.description:
```mojo
var c = CronExpr.parse("0 3 2 * *")          # 03:00 on the 2nd
var t = c.next_fire(now(), Zone.load("America/New_York"))
```

Five fields: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day of month (1-31), month (1-12
or `jan`-`dec`) and day of week (0-7 or `sun`-`sat`, 0 and 7 both Sunday).
A field is a list of `*`, `a`, `a-b`, each with an optional `/step`
(`a/step` runs from `a` to the field's end). `@yearly`, `@annually`,
`@monthly`, `@weekly`, `@daily`, `@midnight` and `@hourly` stand for the
usual expressions.

As in Vixie cron, when both the day of month and the day of week are
restricted (neither starts with `*`), a day matches if either does.

Times are matched on the zone's wall clock. A time that a spring-forward
skips fires at the first moment after the gap, and a time that a fall-back
repeats fires once, at its first occurrence, as Vixie cron and systemd
timers do. An expression that can never match, such as `0 0 30 2 *`, is
refused when it's parsed.

modules.summary: Runs on EC2: a head instance and worker instances per run, started and ended by the scheduler (DESIGN.md, phase 5, PR 5).
modules.description:
With `ORCA_RUNNER=ec2` the scheduler starts a run's start `s` as:

- **a head instance** (`--head-type` at registration, else
  `ORCA_EC2_HEAD_TYPE`, on-demand): the dista head, for a pipeline with
  tasks, and the driver, `<binary> resume <run>`, beside it on localhost;
- **`workers` worker instances** (`--worker-type`, else
  `ORCA_EC2_WORKER_TYPE`; Spot with `--spot`), for a pipeline with tasks,
  started straight after with `DISTA_HEAD` at the head's private address.

Each is tagged `orca.run`, `orca.start`, `orca.pipeline` and `orca.role`,
told to terminate when it shuts down, and started from user data that runs
the pipeline's image (`ORCA_EC2_MODE=docker`, the default: `docker run
--network host`, after `ORCA_EC2_PREAMBLE`, such as an ECR login) or the
binary itself (`direct`, for the tests' stand-in EC2), then shuts down
(`ORCA_EC2_SHUTDOWN`). The head keeps the driver's output in the run's
`driver.log` (`<binary> keep-log`) before it does.

A pipeline registered with `--workers MIN..MAX` scales: its run starts
`MIN` workers, which may be none, and every tick `scale` reads the head's
demand (`dista status --json`, from port 6390 on the head's private address,
through the pipeline's binary: `<binary> dista-status`, since dista's
sockets can't share orca's binary with flare's) and asks
`dista.scale.decide` what to do. It starts the workers asked for,
up to `MAX`, and drains the ones named with `dista drain`; a drained worker
exits once its work and results have moved, and its instance's script shuts
it down. `ORCA_SCALE_UP_AFTER` (5 s), `ORCA_SCALE_IDLE` (60 s) and
`ORCA_SCALE_STEP` (4) tune the policy. The budget counts `MAX`.

A pipeline's secrets (`--secret NAME=ID`) are read by each instance's
script at start, after the preamble, with `aws secretsmanager
get-secret-value` (`ORCA_SECRET_FETCH` replaces the command, which is given
the ID), exported as NAME, given to the containers, and named in
`ORCA_SECRETS` so that every log orca writes masks them.

Every tick, `sweep` terminates the instances of runs that aren't running at
that start, and those older than `ORCA_RUN_DEADLINE` (a day). Instances get
`ORCA_EC2_DATABASE_URL` as `ORCA_DATABASE_URL` (the control instance's
private address), the warehouse, the logs, the region and the scheduler's

modules.summary: Runs on Kubernetes: a dista cluster per run, made and removed by the scheduler (K8S.md).
modules.description:
With `ORCA_RUNNER=kubernetes`, the scheduler starts a run by creating, in
`ORCA_RUNS_NAMESPACE` (default `orca-runs`), from the image the pipeline
was registered with (`orca register --image`):

| Object | |
|---|---|
| A Job, `orca-<run>-<start>` | the driver: `<binary> resume <run>` |
| A Pod and a Service, `orca-<run>-<start>-head` | the dista head, for a pipeline with tasks |
| `workers` Pods, `orca-<run>-<start>-worker-<i>` | dista's workers, for a pipeline with tasks |

All are labelled `orca.run`, `orca.start` (the run's start count),
`orca.pipeline` and `orca.role`, and the head, its Service and the workers
are owned by the Job, so deleting the Job deletes them. The Job has
`activeDeadlineSeconds` (`ORCA_RUN_DEADLINE`, default a day) and
`ttlSecondsAfterFinished` (10 minutes), and `backoffLimit: 0`, as orca
retries runs itself. The driver reaches Postgres through the Secret
`ORCA_RUN_SECRET` (default `orca-db`, key `url`) in that namespace, and the
head through `DISTA_HEAD`; the scheduler's variables named in
`ORCA_RUN_ENV` are copied to every pod.

Every tick, `sweep` deletes the objects of a run that isn't running at that
start any more, and those of a Job that has finished, first appending its
driver pod's log to the run's `driver.log` under `ORCA_LOGS`: what's left after a
run ends, a run restarted on a new cluster, and what a scheduler that was
killed left behind. Pods ask for `ORCA_DRIVER_CPU`, `ORCA_HEAD_CPU` and
`ORCA_WORKER_CPU` (default 500m, 250m and 1) and `ORCA_POD_MEMORY` (512Mi)
each; `cpu_millis` is a run's total, which the scheduler checks against
`ORCA_VCPU_BUDGET` before making a cluster.

modules.summary: Lineage: which snapshots a dataset's snapshot was made from, and what was made from it, from the reads and commits every attempt records.
modules.description:
```
orca lineage lake.report            the latest snapshot's, back and forward
orca lineage lake.report 4417...    one snapshot's
```

A snapshot that an orca attempt committed is **made** by that attempt: its
run, pipeline, step, partition and code, and the snapshots it read, its
**inputs**. The walks go over those edges in SQL (recursive CTEs):

- **`back`** from a snapshot: the attempt that made it, then the attempts
  that made each of its inputs, and so on, to inputs no orca attempt made
  (sources: a table written by something else, or a read of a dataset
  before it had any snapshot, which isn't listed).
- **`forward`** from a snapshot: every snapshot made by an attempt that read
  it, then what was made from those, and so on.

Both stop at `depth` steps (default 20), so a deep graph is cut rather than
slow. A snapshot recorded by two attempts (a retry that recognised its
earlier attempt's commit) is listed once, as the nearer and earlier. Only
datasets take part: a table outside the warehouse has no name to follow.
The same edges are in the snapshots' own summaries, as `orca.reads`.

`<ORCA_LOGS>/<pipeline>/<run>/<step>/<partition>/<attempt>.log` (the

where the log ends up, which `read_location` reads either way.

environment variables that hold a run's secrets (`orca register --secret`),

comptime Taxi = Pipeline["taxi", Download, Load, Compact]

A pipeline is partitioned by month unless it says otherwise with

or a `Seq` of them for a gather step.

Steps are listed after the step they follow, so the declared order is a
valid run order; `check` asserts it at compile time, along with every edge's
types and unique names. Every function that runs a pipeline calls `check`,
so a pipeline that breaks a rule doesn't compile.

reports each attempt to a `Store`, either `MemoryStore` (what `run` uses: a
run lives as long as the process) or `orca.state.PgStore`, which makes a run
resumable. Each step's output is kept encoded by dista's codec, as Postgres
holds it. A step that raises is retried up to its `retries`, then fails its
partition: the steps after it for that partition, and any gather step over
it, are skipped, while other partitions carry on.

    fills=Previous,                                   # last month

wall clock (`Current`), or the one before it (`Previous`, the default): a
monthly load that runs on the 2nd loads the month that just ended.
`catchup=False` tells the scheduler to start only the latest of the fires it
missed while it was down. The scheduler itself is phase 2's next PR; until
then a schedule is declared, checked, and shown by `describe` and `fires`.

modules.summary: The scheduler: fires schedules, senses datasets, queues backfills and rebuilds, and starts runs.
modules.description:
```
orca register ./build/taxi             runs `taxi describe`, records the binary
orca backfill taxi 2011-01..2024-12    a run per partition that isn't done
orca backfill labels @all              keyed: runs of keys_per_run undone keys
orca rebuild taxi.trips 2024-01        the pipelines downstream, in order
orca tick                              one pass, then exits
orca scheduler                         a pass every second
```

The scheduler links no pipeline. It knows one by the `describe` it printed,
kept in `orca.pipelines` with the binary's path, and reads the schedule,
partitions and limits from that JSON in SQL. Everything it decides is in
Postgres, so it can be stopped and restarted, or run twice, at any time:

- **A fire is a row.** `orca.fires` is keyed by (pipeline, fire time), and a
  fire's row and its `queued` run are inserted in one transaction, so a fire
  is never made twice. Fires are counted from the last one recorded (or from
  when the pipeline was registered), so the fires missed while the scheduler
  was down are made once each, or, with `catchup=False`, only the latest.
  A fire whose partition is before the pipeline's first is recorded without
  a run.
- **Starting a run is `resume`.** A queued run has nothing done, or what a
  resume or rerun from `orca ui` left it, which is what `<binary> resume
  <run>` takes (with `--allow-new-code` when the resume said so). The scheduler marks the run `running`,
  with no heartbeat and itself as owner, and execs the binary, which claims
  it. It doesn't wait: the run records its own progress.
- **`max_runs`.** Under a lock on the pipeline's row, the runs that are live
  (a fresh heartbeat, or started by the scheduler less than the stale limit
  ago) are counted, and only that many fewer than `max_runs` are started.
- **Backfills queue what isn't done.** A key is done when every mapped
  step has succeeded for it in a run of the pipeline's current code
  (`DONE_SQL`). A backfill drops the keys that are done or in a queued or
  running run, sorts the rest and queues a run per `keys_per_run` of them.
- **Where runs run.** `ORCA_RUNNER` is `local` (a process here, the
  default), `kubernetes` (a dista cluster of pods per run, `orca.kube`) or
  `ec2` (a head instance and worker instances per run, `orca.ec2`).
- **Sensors and rebuilds** (`orca.sensors`). A sensor pipeline's pass
  looks for snapshots of the datasets it reads, in `orca.commits` on every
  tick and from `<binary> sense` every `ORCA_SENSE_SECONDS`, and queues a
  run, trigger `sensor`, for those it hasn't seen. A keyed sensor's keys
  dataset is sensed too: a new snapshot of it queues the keys that aren't
  done, in runs of `keys_per_run`. Each rebuild queues its
  next level once the one before has succeeded.
- **Retries.** A scheduled, backfilled or sensed run that failed is started again
  after `ORCA_RETRY_SECONDS` (default 60) doubling with each start, plus up
  to a tenth more as jitter, up to `run_retries` times. One whose process
  died (its heartbeat went stale) is started again at once, within the same
  budget. A manual run is never retried by the scheduler. A run asked to
  cancel whose process died ends `cancelled`.

The scheduler's clock is `orca.civil.now`, which `ORCA_NOW` fixes; fire
times and retry times are on it. Heartbeats are on the database's clock.
A run's output goes to `<ORCA_LOGS>/<pipeline>/<run>/driver.log` when
`ORCA_LOGS` is set: written there by a local run, published there when the
process is reaped if `ORCA_LOGS` is in object storage, or kept from the
driver pod's log on Kubernetes (`orca.kube`).

modules.summary: Runs started by datasets: sensors, and rebuilds downstream of a dataset.
modules.description:
```
orca rebuild raw.events 2024-03           every pipeline downstream, in order
```

**Sensors.** A pipeline declared `sensor=True` runs when a dataset it reads
(and doesn't write itself) gets a snapshot. The scheduler learns of one in
two ways (`orca.scheduler`): from `orca.commits`, for a snapshot a
succeeded run of another pipeline committed, and by polling `<binary>
sense` every `ORCA_SENSE_SECONDS` (default 60), for a snapshot something
other than orca committed. `orca.sensed` holds a row per pipeline and
snapshot seen, with the run it started, inserted in the transaction that
queues the run, so a snapshot starts one run however many ticks (or
schedulers) see it. The snapshots a tick sees for one pipeline start one
run, over all the partitions they hold.

A sensor counts from when it's registered as one: the snapshots its
datasets have then are recorded as seen without a run, and commits from
before then are ignored. A backfill or a rebuild covers what came before.

**Partitions.** A snapshot an orca run committed holds the partition of
the step that committed it, or the run's partitions for a gather step. One
committed by something else holds what its summary's `orca.partitions`
says, and without that the downstream pipeline runs the partition its
schedule's next fire would fill now, or, unscheduled, the one now falls in.
`map_keys` moves keys between kinds by containment: a day is the month it's
in, and a month is each of its days. Keys before a pipeline's first
partition are dropped.

**Rebuilds.** `rebuild` queues runs for every pipeline downstream of a
dataset, whether or not it's a sensor, over the keys given, mapped to each
pipeline's kind. A pipeline runs at its longest distance from the dataset
(level 0 reads it), so one that reads two rebuilt datasets runs after both.
The plan is `orca.rebuild_pipelines`; `advance_rebuilds`, on every tick,
queues a level's runs once every run before it has succeeded, and stops at
one that failed or was cancelled, which resuming the run from the UI
continues. A rebuild's commits don't start sensors in pipelines the rebuild
runs itself.

modules.summary: orca's state in Postgres: pipelines, runs, steps and attempts.
modules.description:
Everything lives in the `orca` schema, which `State.migrate` creates and
brings up to date; migrations are SQL in `_migrations`, applied in order
under a transaction-scoped advisory lock, so two processes starting at once
don't both apply one.

**One writer per run.** The process running a run is its `owner` and keeps
`runs.heartbeat` fresh from a thread (`orca.heartbeat`). `State.claim` takes
a run only if its heartbeat is older than the stale limit, or cleared, which
`finish_run` does when a run ends. Every attempt checks in the same
transaction that this process still owns the run, so a process that lost its
run to a resume stops at its next step instead of racing it. The same check
stops a run that was asked to cancel (`runs.cancel_requested`, which `orca
ui` sets) before its next attempt; an attempt already going finishes and is
recorded.

**Each change is one transaction.** Starting an attempt marks its step
running and inserts the attempt; finishing it records the output or the
error on both. A process killed in between leaves an attempt `running`,
which `interrupt` marks failed when the run is resumed.

modules.summary: Steps: the functions a pipeline runs, and the edges between them.
modules.description:
A step wraps a top-level `def` with a name, its input and output types, its
kind, and the step it follows:

```mojo
def download(mut ctx: Ctx, month: Month) raises -> RawFile: ...
def load(mut ctx: Ctx, raw: RawFile) raises -> Loaded: ...
def compact(mut ctx: Ctx, loaded: Seq[Loaded]) raises -> Int64: ...

comptime Download = Step["download", Month, RawFile, download, Mapped]
comptime Load = Step["load", RawFile, Loaded, load, Mapped, after=Download]
comptime Compact = Step["compact", Seq[Loaded], Int64, compact, Gather, after=Load]
```

A mapped step runs once per partition of a run, a gather step once per run.
The edge is checked when the pipeline is compiled:

| Step | Its input must be |
|---|---|
| first, mapped | the pipeline's partition key, such as `Month` |
| first, gather | a `Seq` of the key, every partition of the run |
| mapped, after a mapped step | that step's output |
| gather, after a mapped step | `Seq` of that step's output, one per partition in run order |
| gather, after a gather step | that step's output |

A mapped step can't follow a gather step. Types are compared by their
reflected names, which include their module; the first step's input is
checked by `Pipeline.check`, which knows the key.

A step declares the datasets it reads and writes, as `namespace.table`
names in the warehouse (`orca.tables`):

```mojo
comptime Clean = Step[
    "clean", Month, Int64, clean, Mapped,
    reads=["raw.events"], writes=["lake.events"],
]
```

`orca.tables` refuses a scan of a dataset the step didn't declare in
`reads`, and a commit to one it didn't declare in `writes`, so the graph of
pipelines and datasets that `describe` gives is what the steps do.

modules.description:
```mojo
from orca.tables import append, scan

def load(mut ctx: Ctx, raw: RawFile) raises -> Loaded:
    var src = Table.load_local(raw.table)
    var batches = scan(ctx, src).to_batches()
    var dst = Table.load_local(OUT)
    var id = append(ctx, dst, transform(batches))
    return Loaded(raw.month, id)
```

- **`scan`** reads a table at a pinned snapshot: the one this step's first
  attempt read, or its current snapshot if this is the first attempt, which
  is then recorded. A retry or a resume of the step sees the same data,
  whatever was committed in between.
- **`append`** and **`commit`** put `orca.*` properties in the summary of the
  snapshot they commit (`Ctx.summary`): pipeline, run, step, partition,
  attempt, commit number, code, and the snapshots read. Before writing
  anything, they look through the table's snapshots for one this step
  already made in this run (`Ctx.made`). If an attempt committed and was
  killed before Postgres heard of it, the retry finds that snapshot and
  returns it instead of committing the data a second time.

A table is known by its location, `metadata.location`, and, when it's in
the warehouse, by its dataset name. `ORCA_WAREHOUSE` is the root of a
filesystem catalog: dataset `nyc.trips` is the table at
`<warehouse>/nyc/trips`, where the warehouse is a directory or a location
in object storage (`s3://bucket/warehouse`, as iceberg's `FileIO` reads it,
from the `AWS_*` environment). **`table`** loads a dataset the step declared, and
**`ensure_table`** creates one it writes if it's missing, and adds the
columns the step's schema has and the table lacks. `scan` refuses a
dataset the step didn't declare in `reads=`, and `append` and `commit` one it
didn't declare in `writes=`. A table outside the warehouse (or with
`ORCA_WAREHOUSE` unset) is used by location as before, and belongs to no
dataset.

This module imports iceberg, so only pipelines that use tables build it;
`orca` itself doesn't.

overloads.summary: The table of a dataset the step writes, created empty with `schema` and `spec` if the warehouse doesn't have it yet.
overloads.description:
A table that exists is brought up to `schema`: the columns `schema` has
and the table lacks, matched by name at any depth, are added in one
schema commit, and a column `schema` makes optional becomes optional.
Rows already in the table read the new columns as null. Columns the
table has and `schema` doesn't are kept, and written as null.

It refuses, with the dataset in the message, what that can't do: a
column whose type differs, a new column marked required, a required
column `schema` leaves out, and a field id in `schema` that isn't the
id the table gave that column, since batches built from `schema` carry
its ids and a column is matched by id first. A new column's id should be
the next one up: the table numbers new fields from its highest id, in
the order `schema` lists them, a struct's fields after the struct.
`spec` is only used to create the table.

modules.summary: The dista tasks a pipeline's steps call, and the runtime a run gets.
modules.description:
```mojo
comptime Square = Task[Int, Int, square]
comptime TaxiTasks = Tasks[Square]
comptime Taxi = Pipeline["taxi", Download, Load, tasks=TaxiTasks]

def load(mut ctx: Ctx, raw: RawFile) raises -> Loaded:
    ref rt = ctx.runtime[TaxiTasks]()
    var r = rt.remote[Square](7)
    ...
```

A run of a pipeline with tasks starts one dista `Runtime` before its first
step and keeps it until the run ends: in local mode it forks a head and
`ORCA_WORKERS` workers (default 4); with `DISTA_HEAD` set it joins that
cluster instead. The same binary is dista's worker: run with `DISTA_ROLE`
set, `orca_main` hands the process to dista before reading its arguments.

The runtime starts before orca opens a database connection or its heartbeat
thread, so the forked head and workers inherit neither.

A driver or worker given `DISTA_HEAD` first waits until the head accepts a
connection (`wait_for_head`), trying for a second at a time. On Kubernetes
the head's Service can be a moment old: a connection sent before the node
routes its address waits on a connection-tracking entry that never routes,
for minutes, and dista connects without a timeout. A fresh try each second
gets a fresh entry.

modules.summary: Time zones, from the system's TZif files (RFC 8536).
modules.description:
```mojo
var ny = Zone.load("America/New_York")
var offset = ny.offset_at(utc(2024, 7, 1))   # -14400, EDT
```

A TZif file of version 2 or later lists the zone's transitions as 64-bit
times, each with the UTC offset in force from then on, and ends with a POSIX
`TZ` string (`EST5EDT,M3.2.0,M11.1.0`) that gives the rule after the last
transition. "Slim" files, which some systems install, list transitions only
up to when the current rule began and rely on that string for every year
since; "fat" ones list them to 2037. `Zone` reads both, and a version 1 file,
which has only 32-bit times and no rule. Leap-second records are skipped:
orca's times are POSIX times, as the `right/` zones' aren't.

Files are read from `ORCA_ZONEINFO`, default `/usr/share/zoneinfo`. `UTC`
needs no file.

modules.summary: `orca ui`: pipelines and runs as web pages, and the same as JSON.
modules.description:
```
ORCA_DATABASE_URL=postgresql:///orca ./build/orca ui     # 127.0.0.1:8270
```

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/` | pipelines, with their schedules, next runs and last runs |
| `/pipelines/<name>` | a pipeline's steps, partitions, schedule, next runs and runs; a keyed one's keys, done, live and failed |
| `/pipelines/<name>/keys/<key>` | one key of a keyed pipeline: its steps in every run it was in |
| `/runs` | runs, newest first; `?pipeline=`, `?status=`, `?trigger=` |
| `/runs/<id>` | a run's DAG, steps and partitions, attempts, errors, reads and commits |
| `/runs/<id>/attempts/<attempt>` | an attempt's log, with its error |
| `/runs/<id>/timeline.json` | the run's Dista timeline, for Perfetto |
| `/runs/<id>/driver.log` | the run's driver output, as the scheduler kept it |
| `/datasets` | datasets, with their writers, readers and latest snapshots, and the graph of pipelines and datasets |
| `/datasets/<name>` | a dataset's place in that graph and its snapshots |
| `/datasets/<name>/snapshots/<id>` | a snapshot's lineage, back and forward (`orca.lineage`) |
| `/rebuilds/<id>` | a rebuild's pipelines by level, with their runs (`orca.sensors`) |

And the actions, each a `POST` of a form (see `orca.actions`):

| `POST` | |
|---|---|
| `/pipelines/<name>/runs` | start a run over `partitions` |
| `/pipelines/<name>/backfill` | a run per partition in `partitions` that has none; `rerun=1` for done ones too |
| `/runs/<id>/resume` | queue a failed, cancelled or stalled run again; `allow_new_code=1` confirms new code |
| `/runs/<id>/rerun` | a new run from `step` on, the steps before it copied |
| `/runs/<id>/cancel` | cancel a run, before its next attempt if it's running |
| `/datasets/<name>/rebuild` | rebuild every pipeline downstream over `partitions` |
| `/login`, `/logout` | a session for the actions, as a cookie; `name`, `password`, `next` |

A page of something still going on (a queued or running run, a running
attempt) refreshes its live part every two seconds from a fragment path,
`/runs/<id>/steps` or `/runs/<id>/attempts/<attempt>/log`, which answers
286 once there's nothing more to show, and the page stops asking. That's
the only JavaScript.

Every path answers HTML, or JSON to `Accept: application/json` or
`?format=json`, built from the same rows, so a script and a person see the
same thing. An action answers `303 See Other` to the page of what it made,
or that page's JSON; one refused answers 409 saying why. The UI holds no
state: its actions are rows the scheduler acts on, it connects to Postgres
per request, and it can run beside the scheduler or anywhere else that
reaches the database. `ORCA_UI_ADDR` (`host:port`) moves it; it binds to
localhost unless told otherwise, and a `POST` whose `Origin` (or
`Referer`) isn't the UI's own is refused, so another site's page can't post
to it through a browser. Reading needs no login; once login is on
(`ORCA_UI_LOGIN=required`, or any user added with `orca user add`), every
action needs a session from `/login`, and each one is recorded as its
user's (`orca.auth`), which a run's page shows.

modules.summary: A dataset's current snapshot, read from its table's metadata file without iceberg, for `<binary> sense`.
modules.description:
A dataset `ns.table` is the filesystem catalog's table at
`<ORCA_WAREHOUSE>/ns/table`, as in `orca.tables`. Its current metadata file
is the one `metadata/version-hint.text` names, or else the highest version
under `metadata/`, ties broken by `last-updated-ms`, as iceberg's catalog
finds it. Of that file, `current_snapshot` reads the current snapshot's ID
and two properties of its summary: whether an orca step made it
(`orca.run`), and the partition keys it holds (`orca.partitions`), which a
writer that isn't orca can set too.

The warehouse is a directory or a location in object storage
(`s3://bucket/warehouse`), listed and read through objectstore's
`FileIOResolver`, from the `AWS_*` environment.

orca's pipelines import iceberg only if they use tables, and every binary
answers `sense`, so this reads the JSON itself: just enough of it to walk
objects and arrays to the fields it needs.
